name: Agiorgitiko

lines.s10: Agiorgitiko, Saint George's grape, makes Nemea in the Peloponnese: deep purple, plum and black cherry, with a soft, velvety tannin.
lines.s20: Agiorgitiko is the red grape of Nemea, in the hills south west of Corinth. It is deep in colour and soft in tannin, with plum, black cherry and a touch of cinnamon, easy young and richer after time in oak.
lines.s45: Agiorgitiko takes its name from Saint George, and its home is Nemea, in the north east Peloponnese. It is deep purple, with black plum, black cherry and a touch of cinnamon. The tannin is soft and the feel generous. Altitude shapes it: the warm valley floor gives plush wines, and the cooler hillside villages give firmer, fresher ones. Young Nemea sees little oak, while a Reserve from the slopes takes on vanilla, cedar and tobacco. Pour it with grilled lamb, moussaka or a tomato braise. In Nemea Hercules killed the lion, and the valley's old sweet red was known as the blood of Hercules.
lines.sale: Agiorgitiko carries the colour of a big red with none of the hard edges: black plum, black cherry and a touch of cinnamon on a soft, velvety tannin. Pour it with the lamb or the moussaka, for a table curious about Greek wine.

glass.lead: Black plum, black cherry and a touch of cinnamon in a deep purple glass, generous in body, with a soft, velvety tannin.

ladder.where: The hillside villages such as Koutsi
The valley floor of Nemea, on red clay

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin medium and soft, alcohol medium plus, body medium to full, and deep in colour.

home.home: Nemea, in the north east Peloponnese, where a wine labelled Nemea is Agiorgitiko alone and altitude decides the style: plush from the red clay of the valley floor, firmer and fresher from hillside villages such as Koutsi, bright, late picked reds and much of the rosé from the high plateau.
home.abroad: Outside Greece it is rare, planted by only a handful of growers. At home it also makes rosé and blends with Cabernet Sauvignon, sold as regional wine of the Peloponnese.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, as for a medium red.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl, for a Reserve; an ordinary red wine glass suits a young Nemea.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary for a young Nemea; consider it for a Reserve or a Cabernet blend after a sample.
service.age: Young Nemea within three to five years; a Reserve or Grande Reserve from the slopes ten and more.

with.why: soft tannin and ripe plum beside the char
ripe black plum meets the cinnamon and the béchamel
the wine's cherry and cinnamon suit the sauce
an easy red for grilled, herby pork

labels.means: The Peloponnese appellation for red from Agiorgitiko alone, dry above all, with rare sweet reds.
The national ageing terms; Grande Reserve holds four years at least between oak and bottle.
Regional wine of the same vineyards: Agiorgitiko rosé and blends with Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot.
Village names that may stand beside Nemea: the slopes and the high plateau.

guest.q: How do I say it, and what does it mean?
guest.a: Ah yor YEE tee ko. It means Saint George's grape, and on a list you will often find it simply as Nemea, the place it comes from.
Not this one. Agiorgitiko is deep in colour but soft in tannin, with black plum and black cherry, so a young Nemea drinks easily, even before the food arrives.

guest.q: Why does this blend with Cabernet not say Nemea?
guest.a: A wine labelled Nemea is Agiorgitiko alone. Cabernet Sauvignon stiffens its soft frame and adds blackcurrant, but the blend is sold as regional wine of the Peloponnese.

compare.tell: Xinomavro, from Naoussa in the north, is pale, sharper and far more tannic, with sun dried tomato and black olive; Agiorgitiko is deeper in colour, softer and plusher.
Merlot is as soft and plummy, but often shows cocoa and bay leaf; Agiorgitiko is deeper purple, with sour cherry and a touch of cinnamon.
Sangiovese is paler and tarter, with tomato leaf, dried oregano and a dusty grip; Agiorgitiko is deeper and softer, with black plum and cinnamon.

profile.st: Deep purple to ruby · Body medium to full · Acid medium · Tannin medium, soft and velvety · Alcohol medium plus · Dry
profile.fruit: Black plum, black cherry and sour cherry; strawberry in rosé
profile.other: Cinnamon and clove; vanilla, cedar and tobacco from oak in a Reserve; raisin and dried fig in the rare sweet reds
profile.tell: Deep colour with a soft, velvety tannin, plum and a touch of cinnamon: plush where Xinomavro is pale and sharp
profile.regions: Nemea in the Peloponnese, with regional wine of the Peloponnese and Corinth; rare outside Greece
profile.confuse: Xinomavro is pale, sharp and tannic, with sun dried tomato; Merlot is as soft but often shows cocoa and bay leaf

cards.front: Agiorgitiko: which appellation does it make, and with what other grapes?
cards.back: Nemea, in the north east Peloponnese, and none: a red labelled Nemea is Agiorgitiko alone. Blends with Cabernet Sauvignon are regional wine.

cards.front: How does altitude change Agiorgitiko within Nemea?
cards.back: The warm valley floor on red clay gives plush wines and the old sweet reds; the hillside villages give firmer, fresher wines; the cool high plateau gives bright, late picked reds and much of the rosé.

cards.front: Agiorgitiko: what does its name mean, and what legend belongs to Nemea?
cards.back: Saint George's grape. Nemea is where Hercules killed the lion, and the valley's old sweet red was called the blood of Hercules.

questions.q: A Greek red poured blind is deep purple, with black plum, black cherry and a touch of cinnamon, medium acidity and a soft, velvety tannin. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Deep colour, plum and cherry and a soft tannin mark Agiorgitiko of Nemea. Xinomavro, the nearest miss, is pale and high in acid with a firm grip, and smells of sun dried tomato and black olive.

questions.q: A guest sees a Peloponnese red that blends Agiorgitiko with Cabernet Sauvignon and asks why it is not labelled Nemea. What do you tell her?
opts: Nemea must be a sweet wine
Nemea must come from the coast
questions.exp: A red labelled Nemea is Agiorgitiko alone, so a blend with Cabernet Sauvignon is sold as regional wine. Nemea does allow rare sweet reds, but most of it is dry, so sweetness is the nearest wrong answer.

questions.q: A guest has heard of an old sweet red of Nemea, once called the blood of Hercules, and asks how it was made. What do you tell her?
opts: From sun dried or overripe Agiorgitiko
By adding sugar to the finished dry wine
From grapes frozen on the vine
From grapes touched by noble rot
questions.exp: Nemea's old sweet red came from sun dried or overripe Agiorgitiko, left naturally sweet or fortified. Noble rot, the nearest wrong answer, makes Sauternes and Tokaji, not the sweet reds of Nemea.

sources.title: Neos Kosmos: growing Greek grapes in Australia

report: A new grape, mode home as the plan fixes it. No TASTE row exists, so nothing can contradict TASTE.world.

Nemea Agiorgitiko alone, the three altitudes (valley floor on red clay, hillside villages at 400 to 650 metres such as Koutsi, the plateau of Asprokambos), soft, velvety tannin and medium acidity, little oak young and vanilla, cedar and tobacco in a Reserve, the Grande Reserve's four years, PGI rosé and Cabernet blends, 15 to 17 degrees, lamb, moussaka, pastitsio, souvlaki and a tomato braise, the lion of Hercules and the blood of Hercules all stand on the Codex's own Nemea record. Saint George's grape stands there too and on Wine Enthusiast; the exact derivation, from the old name of Nemea town or from a chapel, is given two ways in the sources and is left out.
The glass names sweet spice as cinnamon and clove, where the Codex's Nemea record says sweet spice; a checker may hold that to a source.

Abroad stands on one newspaper piece that names small trial vineyards in Australia, southern France, the United States and South Africa without naming this grape for each, so the entry says only that it is rare and in a few trial vineyards. The same piece says Provence admitted Agiorgitiko in 2021; one source only, left out.

The Codex's Nemea record calls it Greece's largest red appellation and the most planted red, and the most food friendly Greek red on a list: rankings and a superlative the house rules keep out of new prose.
This session reached search alone; no host could be fetched, so each address is cited as the search results gave it and a checker should open them.

checked.verdict: Sound after six fixes. Nemea's rules, the three bands, the ageing terms and the Hercules story stand; the plateau was given rose and light reds where the Codex's record says growers now make structured Nemea there, abroad rested on trial vineyards one source did not name, and the sale echoed Meunier's and Glera's.
changed: lines.sale: The hook, soft and generous from the first sip, echoed Meunier's easy to love on the first sip, and the pour, the easy way into Greek wine, echoed Glera's easy way to begin. The sale now hooks on deep colour without hard edges and pours for a table curious about Greek wine.

worlds.home.home: The plateau was given rose and light reds, which the Codex's Nemea record calls its past: growers now make structured Nemea there, with bright acid and late harvests, and Asprokambos is named on labels for fresh, structured wine. The second round put bright, late picked reds in place of the freshest, a superlative a reader could take for praise.

worlds.home.abroad: Planted only in a few trial vineyards stood on one newspaper piece that did not name this grape in each place, and other pages name commercial plantings abroad by producers. Rare, planted by only a handful of growers, holds both.
food.with.1.why: Generous fruit named nothing; ripe black plum does, and the cinnamon of a moussaka is the spice the reason meant.
guest.1.a: Plum and cherry fruit leaned on the word fruit; black plum and black cherry, the lead's notes, stand alone.
cards.1.back: The same change as the home line: the plateau gives bright, late picked reds and much of the rose, as the Codex's Nemea record has it.
open: The derivation of Saint George's grape, from a chapel or an old name of Nemea town, stays out.
Provence's admission of Agiorgitiko in 2021 stands on one source and stays out.
